summary: This standards-track RFC defines Seamless Bidirectional Forwarding Detection, a simplified way to use BFD with most negotiation removed. That brings quick provisioning and better control and flexibility for nodes starting path monitoring. It updates RFC 5880.

plainLanguage.summary:
Seamless Bidirectional Forwarding Detection, or S-BFD, is a simpler version of BFD. In ordinary BFD both ends of a link agree on a session before anything can be checked, which takes time and leaves a session running on the far end.

In S-BFD the node that wants to be checked simply reserves a number and advertises it. Any node that knows the number can send a test packet straight away and get an answer back, so the check starts and finishes without any setup. The far end answers with a single stateless session instead of one session per path.

questions: how does s-bfd differ from bfd
subtitle: A stripped-down BFD that tests a path without a session on the far end.

tldr.problem: Ordinary BFD needs both ends of a path to agree a session before any traffic is checked, and the target end has to hold an active session for every path that anyone wants to monitor.
tldr.mechanism: S-BFD keeps the BFD packet but removes most of the negotiation. Each node reserves a number, a discriminator, for the things it wants to be reachable and advertises it through a routing protocol; a reflector session on that node answers any packet carrying that number.
tldr.outcome: A continuity test can start and finish with no setup, and the target node holds one stateless reflector instead of many sessions. The cost is a new discriminator space to keep collision free and a different state machine on the initiator.

today: RFC 7880 is a Proposed Standard from July 2016 that updates RFC 5880, adding the S-BFD mechanism to the base BFD specification. It has not been obsoleted. How S-BFD packets are carried over IPv4, IPv6 and MPLS is defined separately in RFC 7881.

sections.title: What S-BFD Removes From BFD
sections.content:
Bidirectional Forwarding Detection, described in RFC 5880 and related documents, has generalized failure detection for many protocols and applications. This document defines Seamless Bidirectional Forwarding Detection, a simplified mechanism for using BFD with a large proportion of the negotiation aspects eliminated. The stated benefits are quick provisioning and improved control and flexibility for nodes that start path monitoring.

The name comes from the main thing the mechanism removes. In traditional BFD there is a time gap between the moment a node wants to perform a continuity test and the moment the test completes. In BFD terms, the initial change of state from DOWN to UP is virtually nonexistent. Removing this seam gives applications a smooth and continuous operational experience, and the mechanism is built to leverage existing implementations and protocol machinery while providing a simplified and largely stateless infrastructure for continuity testing.

The mechanism is described at the level of the base BFD specification. How S-BFD packets are carried over IPv4, IPv6 and MPLS is left to a separate document, RFC 7881, and further use cases are listed in RFC 7882.
sections.plainLanguage: Ordinary BFD needs both ends to set up a session before any checking can start. S-BFD takes that setup away, so a test can begin the instant somebody decides to run one. That is where the name comes from: there is no seam in the middle.

sections.title: How an S-BFD Test Works
sections.content:
An S-BFD module on each network node allocates one or more S-BFD Discriminators for local entities and creates a Reflector BFD session. Allocated discriminators may be advertised by applications such as OSPF or IS-IS, so that applications on other nodes learn which discriminator a remote node has assigned to a remote entity. When the Reflector BFD session receives an S-BFD Control packet whose Your Discriminator field matches one of the local S-BFD Discriminator values, it sends a response S-BFD Control packet back to the initiator.

Once that setup is in place, any node that knows the discriminator a remote node allocated can run a continuity test by sending S-BFD Control packets with that value in the Your Discriminator field. The RFC works through an example with an IS-IS network. A node with System-ID xxx allocates S-BFD Discriminator 123 and advertises it in an IS-IS TLV; a node with System-ID yyy allocates 456 and advertises that. Both nodes create a Reflector BFD session. When the first node wants to check the reachability of the second, it sends an S-BFD Control packet destined to the second node with the Your Discriminator field set to 456, and the reflector session on the second node sends a response back.

The RFC also flags an open question. When a node allocates several S-BFD Discriminators, there is currently no defined way for remote nodes to work out which discriminator belongs to which entity. The use of several discriminators on one node is therefore discouraged until a way of learning the mapping is defined.
sections.plainLanguage: Each node reserves a number for the things it wants to be reachable and tells the rest of the network about it through a routing protocol. A test is then just one packet sent to that number. The far end looks the number up in its own list and answers.

sections.title: S-BFD Discriminators and Their Pools
sections.content:
A discriminator is the 32-bit field that says which session a BFD packet belongs to. S-BFD uses two of them: the S-BFD Discriminator, allocated for a local entity and listened for by the SBFDReflector, and the BFD Discriminator, allocated for an SBFDInitiator.

An S-BFD Discriminator must be unique within an administrative domain. If two nodes allocate the same value, an S-BFD Control packet can falsely terminate on the wrong node, and the reflector session there will generate a response because a Your Discriminator value matches. The RFC calls this clearly undesirable.

To reduce collisions, the RFC describes two pools. An SBFDInitiator allocates its discriminator from the BFD Discriminator pool, and if the system also supports classical BFD that pool should be shared between SBFDInitiator sessions and classical BFD sessions. An SBFDReflector allocates from the S-BFD Discriminator pool, which should be a separate pool from the BFD Discriminator pool. The reason is that a reflector may allocate values for entities derived from protocol identifiers such as a System-ID or a Router-ID, or from network targets such as an IP address, and those derived values may already be assigned to other BFD sessions.

Even with separate pools a collision is possible between different S-BFD applications that derive values with different algorithms. If two applications use S-BFD for the same purpose, such as network reachability, a colliding value can simply be shared. If they use it for different purposes, the collision has to be addressed.
sections.plainLanguage: The numbers that identify a test must not clash inside one administrative domain, or a packet could be answered by the wrong node. The RFC therefore separates the numbers used by the answering side from the numbers used by the testing side.

sections.title: The Reflector BFD Session
sections.content:
Each network node creates one or more Reflector BFD sessions. Such a session transmits an S-BFD Control packet in response to a received S-BFD Control packet whose Your Discriminator field carries an S-BFD Discriminator allocated for a local entity. It has three defining characteristics. It must not transmit any S-BFD packets based on local timer expiry, so it never starts a session of its own. It must transmit an S-BFD Control packet in response to a received packet with a valid S-BFD Discriminator in the Your Discriminator field, unless a local policy such as an administrative, security or rate-limiter rule prohibits it. And it must be capable of sending only two states, UP and AdminDown.

One reflector session may handle packets targeted at all locally allocated discriminators, or a few sessions may each handle a subset. Which arrangement to use is a local matter and outside the scope of the document.

Demultiplexing works with lower-layer information, such as the dedicated destination UDP port of RFC 7881 or the associated Channel Type of RFC 7885. If the packet is an S-BFD packet for a reflector, it is looked up by the Your Discriminator value in the table of S-BFD Discriminators. Otherwise it is looked up in the table of BFD Discriminators to find an SBFDInitiator session or a classical BFD session; with no match the packet is discarded, and if the match is a classical BFD session the packet is discarded as well.

The responder verifies the validity of received packets as described in RFC 5880. If the Your Discriminator field is not one of the entries allocated for local entities, the packet must be discarded. Otherwise the packet belongs to the reflector session responsible for that discriminator, and that session should transmit a response if local policy allows.

Most fields of the response are copies of the received packet. The Detect Mult, Desired Min TX Interval, and the two discriminator fields are all swapped across. Two fields differ from the base specification. The Demand bit is set to 0, to show that the packet came from the reflector. The Required Min RX Interval is set to the reflector's own minimum interval, and the reflector controls how fast initiators send to it by choosing a value that reflects the current load. The Required Min Echo RX Interval is set to the minimum receive interval the session supports, or to 0 if the device does not loop back echo packets.

Two further rules matter. If the monitored local entity is in service, the state in the response must be UP; if it is temporarily out of service, the state should be AdminDown. And if the reflector receives an S-BFD Control packet with the Demand bit cleared, the packet must be discarded, which is what stops a reflected packet from being reflected back.
sections.plainLanguage: The answering side runs one session that never starts anything by itself and only ever reports two states: working or temporarily out of service. It copies most of the fields of the packet it receives and swaps the two discriminator numbers, and it can ask the sender to slow down by advertising a longer minimum interval.

sections.title: The Initiator State Machine and the Loop Problem
sections.content:
An SBFDInitiator can be a persistent session with a transmission timer, which the RFC calls a stateful initiator, or it can be a module, a script or a tool that sends one or more S-BFD Control packets when needed, which is a stateless initiator. For a stateless initiator a complete BFD state machine may not apply at all.

For a stateful initiator the state machine of RFC 5880 does not work, because the reflector session only ever sends UP and AdminDown and so never sends the INIT state. The RFC therefore gives a recommended state machine with three states: ADMIN DOWN, DOWN and UP. The notation on each arc gives the state of the initiator, as received in the State field of an S-BFD Control packet, or indicates the expiration of the detection timer. The timer in the ADMIN DOWN state moves the session to DOWN. A packet received with the state UP moves the session from DOWN to UP. Expiration of the detection timer moves it back to DOWN, and the ADMIN DOWN timer moves it to ADMIN DOWN.

The initiator sets the Demand bit to 1 always, to show that the packet came from an initiator, puts the discriminator of the remote entity in the Your Discriminator field, and sets the Required Min RX Interval and Required Min Echo RX Interval to 0. Every initiator must have a locally unique My Discriminator taken from the BFD Discriminator pool.

When the initiator receives a valid response it should conclude that the packet reached the intended remote entity. If the state in the response is AdminDown, the initiator must not conclude that reachability is lost and must back the packet transmission interval off to no faster than one second. When enough packets have not arrived as they should, the initiator should declare loss of reachability to the remote entity; the criteria and the resulting action are outside the scope of the document, and the action may be logging an error. An implementation must also not expect the very first response to arrive instantly, since the time is the sum of the latencies from initiator to responder and back.

Appendix A works through a loop that this design has to avoid. Suppose two nodes each reserve a discriminator and each run a reflector in listening mode. If someone in the middle injects a spoofed packet whose discriminators and addresses match both nodes, the reflector on one node swaps them and sends it back, the reflector on the other node does the same, and because reflectors must set the TTL of reflected packets to 255 the packet bounces between them forever. One malicious packet is enough. The solution is the Demand bit: the initiator always sets it and the reflector always clears it, so a node can tell that a packet is already a reflected packet and does not reflect it again. For the same reason, an initiator must discard any S-BFD Control packet that arrives with the Demand bit set.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender keeps three states instead of the four that ordinary BFD uses, because the far end never reports the handshake state. The Demand bit is what makes this safe: the sender marks its packets and the receiver clears the mark, so a packet that has already been answered is recognized and not answered again.

sections.title: Operational Considerations
sections.content:
S-BFD gives a smooth and continuous experience as an operations, administration and maintenance mechanism for connectivity checking and connection verification, because the simplification removes negotiation and therefore makes provisioning faster and simpler.

The simplification also brings a risk. Because there is no setup, a misconfiguration can make an SBFDInitiator send S-BFD Control packets to a target that does not exist, or that is outside the S-BFD administrative domain. Where a persistent initiator is used, a deployment should ensure that S-BFD Control packets do not propagate for an extended period outside the administrative domain that uses it. Operational measures should also detect the case where responses stop arriving for a long time and remediate it. The RFC notes that dynamic advertisement of S-BFD discriminators and automation checks before applying configurations largely mitigate these concerns.

The scaling benefit comes from the number of reflectors. The mechanism removes the need for egress nodes to have fully active BFD sessions when only one side wants to run continuity tests, and with the reflector concept egress no longer has to create active BFD sessions on a per-path, per-LSP or per-function basis. The total number of BFD sessions in the network is reduced.

Congestion needs care. When S-BFD performs failure detection it consumes bandwidth and CPU, so operators must provision the rates at which S-BFD packets are sent correctly. Where BFD is used across multiple hops a congestion control mechanism must be implemented, and when congestion is detected the BFD implementation must reduce the traffic it generates. The exact detection mechanism is out of scope, and may include the detection of lost BFD Control packets. A reflector can limit how fast initiators send to it by using the Required Min RX Interval, at the cost of a longer detection time.

S-BFD co-exists with classical BFD sessions, because the demultiplexing requirements for the initial packet distinguish the two.
sections.plainLanguage: The savings come from the far end no longer holding a session for every path. The risk is that with no setup there is nothing to catch a mistake, so a test can be sent to a target that does not exist or to a place outside the network that owns it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The same security considerations as those in RFC 5880 apply. The RFC then lists measures that strengthen them.

The initiator may pick the sequence number carried in the authentication section based on the configured authentication mode. The reflector must not use the cryptographic sequence number to decide whether to accept a packet, because the reflector keeps no peer state and may receive S-BFD packets from several initiators. It may use the Auth Key ID in the incoming packet to verify the Authentication Data, and it must accept the packet if authentication succeeds. When it answers, it must compute the Authentication Data using the same sequence number it received. The initiator should accept a packet whose sequence number falls within the permissible range, and one possible procedure is the one described in the BFD generic cryptographic authentication work in progress.

Used this way, reflectors remain stateless despite using security. They are not susceptible to replay attacks, because they always respond whatever sequence number the packet carries, and an attacker cannot impersonate the responder, because the initiator only accepts packets carrying the sequence number it originally used.

The RFC strongly encourages the use of strong forms of authentication for S-BFD. Simple Password authentication potentially puts other services at risk, because S-BFD packets can be intercepted and the same password values reused elsewhere.
sections.plainLanguage: The reflector answers whoever asks, so it cannot judge a packet by its sequence number the way a normal session would. Instead it always replies with the sequence number it was given, which keeps it stateless and hard to fool, while the sender checks that the reply carries the number it sent.

items.title: Fewer sessions
items.text: The egress node no longer needs an active BFD session for every path, label-switched path or function it serves.

items.title: Misconfiguration risk
items.text: An initiator can send S-BFD packets to a target that does not exist or that lies outside the administrative domain.

items.title: Congestion control
items.text: A congestion control mechanism must be implemented when BFD runs across multiple hops, and traffic must be reduced when congestion is detected.

items.title: Rate control
items.text: A reflector can slow initiators down through the Required Min RX Interval, at the cost of a longer detection time.

viz.caption: What the reflector can and cannot check

items.title: Stateless answering
items.text: The reflector keeps no peer state, so it can answer packets from many different initiators.

items.title: No sequence-number decisions
items.text: The reflector must not use the cryptographic sequence number to decide whether to accept a packet.

items.title: Same number back
items.text: When it answers, the reflector must reuse the sequence number it received.

items.title: Strong authentication
items.text: The RFC strongly encourages strong authentication, since Simple Password values may be reused by other services.
